10-reguli-simple-protejare-date-personal.excerpt: A practical guide for anyone who wants to reduce their digital risks and avoid identity theft, phishing and data leaks.
10-reguli-simple-protejare-date-personal.title: 10 simple rules to protect your personal data online
10-reguli-simple-protejare-date-personal.meta_description: Ten practical habits to reduce exposure of personal data, secure accounts and limit the risk of online fraud.
10-reguli-simple-protejare-date-personal.content:
1. Use unique and strong passwords

Avoid the same password for multiple accounts. If a service is compromised, attackers often try the same email and password combination on other platforms.

Choose long, hard-to-guess passwords. Ideally, use a password manager that can generate and store different passwords for each account.

2. Enable two-step authentication

Even if your password is compromised, two-step authentication adds an extra layer of protection. Enable it for email, social networks, banking apps, and any account that contains important information.

Prefer authentication apps or passkeys when the service supports them.

3. Beware of suspicious emails and messages

Do not automatically open links or attachments received from unknown sources. Check the sender's real address and be wary of messages that try to create panic or pressure you to take immediate action.

4. Check app permissions

Many apps request access to your camera, microphone, contacts, or location. Periodically check permissions and disable access that is not needed.

5. Constantly update devices and apps

Updates don't just bring new features. They frequently include security patches that fix vulnerabilities that can be exploited by attackers.

6. Don't publish too much personal information

Date of birth, location, phone number, address or holiday details can be used for social engineering attacks.

7. Use secure connections

Avoid entering sensitive information on unknown public Wi-Fi networks. Check if the site uses HTTPS.

8. Protect your phone

Use PIN, Face ID or fingerprint. Configure the remote wipe and locate features provided by the operating system.

9. Back up important data

Keep copies of important documents in multiple locations. Ideal: local device, cloud and separate backup.

10. Check accounts regularly

Delete accounts you no longer use. Revoke unknown sessions and devices and regularly check activity on important accounts.

Small habits, repeated consistently, reduce the risk of account and data compromise.

cum-recunosti-email-phishing.excerpt: The telltale signs of fraudulent messages and the steps to take if you've opened a suspicious link.
cum-recunosti-email-phishing.seo_title: How to recognize a phishing email
cum-recunosti-email-phishing.title: How to recognize a phishing email
cum-recunosti-email-phishing.meta_description: Learn to check the sender, links and urgent requests, and what steps to take after a phishing message.
cum-recunosti-email-phishing.content:
Phishing is an attempt to get you to reveal information, send money, or install dangerous software. The message can come via email, SMS, social media or chat apps and impersonate a company or person you trust.

What does a phishing message look like?

Sometimes the sender uses a fake address or a domain very similar to the real one. A changed letter, a different extension or hard-to-see characters can make the difference. The display name does not confirm the identity of the sender: check the full address.

Alarmist messages are another signal. "Account will be closed today", "payment failed" or "parcel is blocked" can push you to act without verification. Attackers also use unexpected rewards or fake invoices to get you to open an attachment.

Fake links and pages

A button may display convincing text but lead to another address. On your computer, hover over the link to see the destination; on the phone, long press without unlocking. Do not enter your password after arriving from an unsolicited link. Open the app manually or type in the known address.

Fake login pages can copy the appearance of a legitimate service. It checks the domain, the HTTPS connection and whether the page was opened by you. HTTPS encrypts the connection, but does not guarantee that the site is legitimate.

What information is not requested by messages

A legitimate bank or service should not ask for your full password, the unique code received by SMS or the recovery code. Be careful with urgent financial requests, including those from a known person: their account may be compromised. Confirm through a separate channel.

How to check a message

  • Examine the full address of the sender and the domain of the links.
  • Contact the organization using the official number or application.
  • Do not open unexpected attachments, especially archives and executable files.
  • Look for mistakes, unusual wording and time pressure, without relying only on them.
  • Report the message as phishing and delete it after verification.

Attachments can hide dangers

A document that looks like an invoice, resume or delivery confirmation may contain a fake login link or try to install unwanted software. Don't enable macros or install apps just to "view the document". If you're not expecting the file, confirm with the sender using an already known conversation, not replying to the suspicious message.

Attacks can be personalized with your name, job, or a recent purchase. These details do not prove that the message is genuine; they may come from public information or an older leak. Even a well-written message should be checked when it asks for sensitive actions.

Habits that reduce risk

Enable two-step authentication, use different passwords, and keep your browser and system up to date. A password manager can deny autofill on a bogus domain, providing a useful hint. Report suspicious messages through the email service function; at work, follow IT department procedure and do not forward the attachment to colleagues.

If you clicked on the link

If you just opened the page and didn't provide any data, close it and run a security check on your device. If you've entered a password, change it immediately from the official website or app, and change it anywhere else it's been reused. Enable two-step authentication and revoke unknown sessions.

If you have provided bank details or authorized a payment, contact your bank immediately using the number on your card or the official app. Keep the message for reporting and notify IT if the incident involves a work account. If you have installed a file, disconnect the device from the network and seek trusted technical help before using it for important accounts.

Pausing for a few seconds to check can prevent loss and unauthorized access. You don't need to respond immediately to a message claiming to be urgent: check through an independent channel.

An example of step-by-step verification

You receive a message about a package and you are asked for a small fee for delivery. Instead of opening the button, check the order number in the store's app or on the courier's website by typing the address yourself. If you have not placed an order, there is no reason to follow the instructions in the message. The same principle applies to bank alerts: open the official app and look for the notification there.

Don't rely on the logo, colors or signature in the email. These are easily copied. The fact that the message appears in an old thread is no guarantee either; attackers can compromise an address and continue real conversations. A new request for money or a change of bank account must be confirmed verbally to a number you had already saved.

In organizations, attacks can use the name of a manager and ask for gift cards, urgent transfers or internal documents. Follow the normal approval steps even if the message claims to be an exception. If in doubt, report the message and ask the IT team without replying to the sender.

Quick reporting helps other people too. Use the vendor's phishing reporting tool or forward the message to the responsible team according to local procedure. Do not publish personal data from the message on social networks; keep only the information necessary for the investigation.

date-personale-nu-posta-online.excerpt: Find out what information can be used for identity theft, fraud, and unauthorized access.
date-personale-nu-posta-online.seo_title: What personal data not to post online
date-personale-nu-posta-online.title: What personal information you should never post online
date-personale-nu-posta-online.meta_description: Find out what personal data, documents and location details can increase the risk of identity theft and how to protect them.
date-personale-nu-posta-online.content:
A post can reach far beyond the audience you see at the time. The copied information can be used for identity theft, fraud, accessing accounts or finding out when the home is empty. Think about posting the same detail on a public board.

Documents and Identifiers

The CNP is a sensitive identifier that can be associated with other data for impersonation attempts. Do not publish it and only provide it when there is a legitimate reason through a secure channel.

Certificate and passport copies include photo, document numbers and other details useful for fraud. Do not post images that are even partially visible; remove copies from public spaces and use a watermark with the purpose and date when you need to send them to a trusted organization.

Bank card, front or back, can reveal the number, expiration date and security code. Do not photograph the card or transmit authorization codes.

Home, contact and travel

Exact address may facilitate harassment or an unwanted visit. Avoid associating it with photos that show the entrance or daily routine. Personal phone number can be used for spam, account takeover attempts or fraudulent messages; limit who can see it.

Boarding passes and QR tickets can contain scannable codes and travel data. Cover the codes and details completely before you post a photo. Real-time location reveals where you are and when you're away. Turn off public sharing and post vacation photos after you're back.

Vacation details, such as departure dates and duration, can signal that your home is empty. Keep plans for your inner circle.

Children and family information

Photos and details about children can reveal their school, schedule, places attended and names used in the family. Ask for age-appropriate consent and avoid uniforms with visible logos, name tags, or real-time location.

Digital Secrets

Passwords, recovery codes, and screenshots of them are not published or sent in chat. A single code can give an attacker immediate access.

Answers to security questions can be guessed from your public profile: hometown, pet's name or school. Choose unique answers, keep them in a password manager and don't disclose them.

Forms and private conversations

A job offer, contest or online test may ask for more data than necessary. Check who organizes the form, why they need each detail and where they send it. Don't send documents to unknown accounts just because the message seems personalized.

Screenshots from conversations may expose names, profile photos, phone numbers, or notifications left at the top of the screen. Before you share a snippet, remove these details and ask others for permission when the conversation is private.

Before you hit 'public'

Check your photo's background, location metadata, visible notifications, and people captured. Audience settings are useful, but do not prevent screenshots or redistribution. If you've accidentally published sensitive data, delete the post, request the removal of duplicates, and change credentials or contact your bank, if applicable.

You can limit your profile's audience, review tags before they appear publicly, and disable automatic location addition to photos. Please review these options after app updates, as settings may change or new controls may appear.

There is no single setting that makes a post completely private. Even in a closed group, a member can save or redistribute the material. Share only what is necessary and choose a level of detail that you would consider acceptable if the post were to become public.

Share only what is necessary. A more discreet profile gives you more control over your identity.

Why information is combined

A single detail may seem innocuous, but multiple posts can create a surprisingly accurate profile. A photo identifies the venue, a comment shows regular hours, and an anniversary suggests information sometimes used to verify accounts. Scammers can use these clues to write credible messages to you or your loved ones.

Public information can be copied even if you delete it later. Search engines, archives, screenshots, and redistributions may retain fragments. That's why the most effective time to limit exposure is before publishing, and periodically reviewing profiles helps reduce old details.

Separate public accounts from personal accounts and use restricted audience settings for photos and family updates. Disable the options that allow you to find your profile by phone number or automatically sync your phonebook if you don't need them. Also check apps connected to social networks and revoke access to those you no longer use.

If a document needs to be sent, ask if a copy with certain fields masked is enough. Submit it through an official portal, not through a link received unexpectedly. For kids, talk to your family about what photos can be posted and avoid revealing their full name, school, and routine in the same post.

A simple rule is to not post real-time information that could help someone locate you or access your accounts. When in doubt, keep the detail private and ask the person concerned for advice.

cum-recunosti-sms-fals-fraude-mesaje.excerpt: Messages about blocked parcels, overdue fees or suspended accounts can be smishing attempts. Learn how to verify the sender and link, and what to do if you've opened the page or entered data.
cum-recunosti-sms-fals-fraude-mesaje.seo_title: How to recognize a fake SMS and avoid smishing
cum-recunosti-sms-fals-fraude-mesaje.title: How to recognize a fake SMS and avoid text fraud
cum-recunosti-sms-fals-fraude-mesaje.meta_description: Learn to recognize fake SMS about parcels, taxes or accounts and to react if you opened a link or entered data.
cum-recunosti-sms-fals-fraude-mesaje.content:
A fake SMS tries to get you to click a link, pay a small amount, or provide account information. Text message attacks are called smishing — a form of phishing that uses SMS or messaging apps. A single clue does not prove that the message is fraudulent; check the sender, context, link and requested action together.

Frequently encountered fake messages

A "parcel blocked" message may ask for a small rescheduling fee and card number. Another claims that you have a debt, that your account is suspended, or that you need to confirm a payment. The scammer is after either the login data, the card data, or the installation of an application that gives access to the phone.

The sender may appear under the name of a known company, and the conversation may end up in the same thread as genuine messages if the identifier has been spoofed or reused. The display name does not authenticate the message. Do not reply or use the phone number or link in the message to verify the story.

Warning signals

  • Requests payment via a short link, unusual transfer or card details, even though you don't have a pending order.
  • Presses you with a very short deadline, threatens to suspend your account or promises an unexpected prize.
  • The website address contains mistakes, extra words or a domain that does not belong to the organization.
  • You are asked for your password, unique code, PIN or to install an application from a link received by message.

HTTPS indicates an encrypted connection, not the fact that the page belongs to the claimed company. On your phone you can long press a link to see its destination without opening it; for more secure verification, close the message and manually enter the official application or type the known address. If there is a real order, check it in the merchant's account or contact the service through its separately published data.

If you opened the link

If you just visited the page and did not enter anything or install anything, close the tab, do not accept site notifications and do not download files. Update your browser and system. A scan may be appropriate if you have downloaded or installed something; simply opening a link does not automatically confirm that the phone has been compromised.

If you have entered a password, change it immediately from the app or official page, from a device that you have no concrete reason to believe is compromised. Change it and wherever you've reused it, enable two-step authentication and revoke unknown sessions. If you have entered the card data or authorized a payment, call the bank using the number on the card or in the official application and ask for instructions to block or contest the operations. Do not wait for the sender's response.

What you can do preventively

Use a password manager: the autofill should stop on a different domain than the real one, which can be a helpful hint. Disable previews that show codes on the lock screen if the phone is in use by other people. Report the message through carrier or platform tools, and for a cyber incident, consult official DNSC channels. Keep the catch and the suspicious address if you report; do not redistribute it as an active link warning.

fraude-online-frecvente-romania-protecti.excerpt: Online frauds use urgent messages, non-existent stores, fake ads and fake identities. The guide shows how to check claims and payments and what steps to take after a suspicious online transaction.
fraude-online-frecvente-romania-protecti.seo_title: Frequent online fraud in Romania: signs and protection
fraude-online-frecvente-romania-protecti.title: The most common online frauds in Romania and how to protect yourself
fraude-online-frecvente-romania-protecti.meta_description: Recognize phishing, fake stores, impersonation and ad scams. Find out how to check an offer and what to do after a fraud.
fraude-online-frecvente-romania-protecti.content:
Online fraud doesn't come in one form. Sometimes a message impersonates a bank, courier or institution; other times an ad leads to a store that doesn't deliver, a fake ad kicks you off the platform, or a supposed consultant promises surefire earnings. The common goal is to obtain money, card data, access to accounts or control of the device. Check each request through a channel you find independently.

Phishing and Impersonation

A message can announce a declined payment, a fine, a blocked package or a security issue. The link opens a page similar to the real one, where you are asked for your password and authorization code. Institutions do not need you to send them via SMS. Close the message and check directly in the official application; if you are contacted by phone, call back to the number published on the institution's website.

False shops and ads

A price well below the market, urgent payment outside the platform, lack of clear data about the merchant or hard-to-find return rules justify caution. Neither reviews nor HTTPS alone guarantee that the seller is legitimate: reviews can be fabricated, and HTTPS only encrypts the connection. Search for the merchant name along with terms like "complaint" and check their contact details, return policy and payment method before ordering.

On ad platforms, a fake buyer can send a "cash out" link or courier, asking for card details and the code received from the bank. To receive a payment you do not have to disclose your online banking security code, PIN or password. Stay in the messaging and payment system of the platform, where there is protection for the transaction.

Investments, technical support and money recovery

An offer that promises guaranteed returns or requires you to install a remote access application is worth checking out separately. It does not send additional money to "unlock" earnings and does not allow a stranger to control your phone or computer. After a loss, there may be people who claim to recover the funds against an advance; no intermediary can guarantee recovery.

Protective steps

  1. Stop the conversation and do not use the contact data received in the message.
  2. Check the offer on the official website or directly in the application.
  3. Pay using a method that provides dispute procedures; read the provider's conditions.
  4. Keep the invoice, announcement, conversation, transfer confirmation and captures.
  5. If you made a suspicious payment, contact the bank immediately; if you have provided access data, change passwords and revoke sessions.

The availability of a refund depends on the payment method, transaction authorization, contract with the supplier and circumstances. Report the announcement in the platform and ask for guidance from the relevant institutions. For cyber incidents, DNSC provides official reporting channels; for a possible crime, keep the evidence and contact the Police.

cum-identifici-site-fals-date-personale.excerpt: A fake page can copy the identity of a bank or store. Check the domain, contact method, and link context before entering your password, card details, or personal information online.
cum-identifici-site-fals-date-personale.seo_title: How to Spot a Fake Site Before Login
cum-identifici-site-fals-date-personale.title: How to identify a fake site before entering personal data
cum-identifici-site-fals-date-personale.meta_description: Check Domain, HTTPS, Merchant Data and Links Before to enter data on a website that may be false.
cum-identifici-site-fals-date-personale.content:
A fake site tries to look familiar enough for you to enter a password, bank code, or contact information. It can copy the logo, colors and forms of a bank or store, but send the information to the attacker. Verification should start with the exact address and why you got there, not the layout of the page.

Check the domain, not just the logo

Read the domain letter by letter and look for substitutions, added words, unusual hyphens, or different endings. A company name can appear in a subdomain of a foreign domain: the text on the left does not say who controls the parent domain. On the phone, the address bar can be shortened; tap it to see the full address. For important accounts, use a previously saved bookmark or the official app.

What HTTPS tells you and what it doesn't tell you

HTTPS encrypts the traffic between the browser and the server and helps prevent interception en route. It does not check if the company is real, if the offer is honest, or if the domain was not registered by a scammer. The lock icon is not a commercial certification. If your browser displays a certificate warning, do not bypass it to get to a payment page.

Check merchant and request

When making a purchase, look for the legal name, working contact details, delivery and return conditions and consistent descriptions. Search separately for the store name plus "complaint" or "fraud"; results may help, but absence of complaints does not prove legitimacy. Improbably low prices, re-starting counts and insistence on direct transfer are reasons to hold off on paying.

An unexpected login page should be treated with caution, even if it uses the brand you know. Banks and platforms may ask for legitimate in-app confirmations, but don't pass on unique codes or passwords to a person who contacted you. If in doubt, close the page and start the session from the known application.

A short list before you send data

  1. Did you initiate access to the site or did you follow an unsolicited link?
  2. Does the full domain match the official address you usually use?
  3. Can you confirm the offer through an independent channel?
  4. Are you being asked for data that is not necessary for the action, such as your PIN or authorization code?
  5. Are the payment method and return policy clearly explained?

If you entered a password, change it from the official website and update all accounts where it was reused. If you have submitted bank details, contact the bank immediately. Keep the address and message for reporting, but do not upload personal data to a public link analysis service.

ce-faci-dupa-link-phishing.excerpt: The reaction depends on what happened after clicking on the link. It separates simple visiting from entering a password, authorizing a payment or installing a file and follows the appropriate steps in each case safely.
ce-faci-dupa-link-phishing.seo_title: Have you accessed a phishing link? What to do
ce-faci-dupa-link-phishing.title: What to do if you clicked on a phishing link
ce-faci-dupa-link-phishing.meta_description: Learn what to do after you've opened a phishing link, entered a password, authorized a payment, or installed a file.
ce-faci-dupa-link-phishing.content:
Opening a link does not automatically mean that your phone or computer has been compromised. The risk depends on what you did on the page and whether you downloaded or installed anything. Close the page and calmly reconstruct the steps: did you enter a password, a code received by SMS, card data or approve a request? Have you installed an app or profile? The answer changes the order of the measures.

If you just visited the page

Close the tab and don't click on notifications, download windows or "clean" buttons. Delete unknown downloads without opening them, update your browser and system, and run the built-in security check if you've downloaded a file. Just accessing the page, in the absence of other clues, does not confirm that malware has been installed. Avoid tools that promise to fix your device immediately and ask for money or remote access.

If you entered your password or code

From a secure session, manually log into the legitimate service and change the password. If the same password was used elsewhere, change it there as well, starting with your primary email address and financial accounts. Enable MFA or a passkey where available, check address and recovery methods, revoke sessions/devices you don't recognize, and remove connected apps you haven't authorized. Do not delete security emails; they can help establish the time of the incident.

A single-use code can authorize a login or transaction; don't dictate it or insert it into an open page in the message. If you sent it, treat the account as urgent: use the official recovery and contact the service through its known channels.

If you entered card details or approved a payment

Call the bank immediately using the number on the card or its official application. It says what data you entered and whether you confirmed a transaction. Asks to evaluate the blocking of the card, of online access or contesting the operation; the steps and rights depend on the type of payment and the specific situation. Check recent transactions and keep the referral number and confirmations.

If you installed an application or file

Do not use the affected device for banking until you have verified it. If an unknown person has received remote access, temporarily disconnect the device from the network and contact the bank from another phone. Only uninstall the app if you know how to do it safely; for persistent symptoms, ask for reliable technical help. Preserve the evidence and report the incident to DNSC or the Police, depending on its nature.

Changing all passwords on the same suspect device can expose accounts again. Secure your device first or use a different one, then check your sessions and recovery methods. Write down what happened and when; this timeline helps the bank and services to respond faster.

verificare-email-compromis-brese-date.excerpt: An address found in a breach doesn't show by itself if someone got into your account. Check notifications and activity, use a reputable search service, and change reused passwords.
verificare-email-compromis-brese-date.seo_title: How to check if your email is in a breach
verificare-email-compromis-brese-date.title: How to check if your email address has been compromised
verificare-email-compromis-brese-date.meta_description: Check your email address in known breaches, understand what the result means and secure your passwords and accounts reused.
verificare-email-compromis-brese-date.content:
You can check if an email address appears in a known breach, but the result doesn't tell you on its own whether someone is controlling your inbox. A breach can expose addresses, names, old passwords, or other fields, depending on the service. Sometimes the data set is incomplete or labeled as unverified. Use the result as a reason to check the accounts, not as a definitive diagnosis.

How to verify without exposing your password

I just enter the email address in a known service like Have I Been Pwned and read the explanation about the incident. The service shows which known vulnerabilities include the address; it won't tell you the associated password. Don't enter your current password into a site that promises to check if it's been stolen or download credential lists.

Also check your inbox for genuine security alerts, login activity, and devices in your account settings. Access the security page by typing the official address yourself. Messages like "your account has been hacked, pay now" can be scams themselves and do not prove that the sender has access to the account.

If the address appears in a gap

Identifies the service and the date of the breach, then changes the password on that service. If your password has been reused, change it on all those accounts, starting with your primary email, banking, and accounts that can recover other accounts. Choose unique passwords generated and stored in a manager. Do not add simple variations of the same password.

Enable two-step authentication or a passkey. Checks recovery number and address, email forwarding rules, filters, connected apps and active sessions. An attacker who created a rule to hide alerts can still be present even after changing the password. Close sessions you don't recognize and update recovery codes.

What information can be exposed?

Some incidents include only the email address and public information; others may include names, phone numbers, purchase history or hashed passwords. Don't assume all fields have been exposed just because the address appears in a result. Read the incident description and service notification. A compromised address can increase the risk of targeted messages, but it doesn't automatically mean identity theft.

Verification limits

The absence of the address from a service does not prove that the data was never exposed: the service may not know about the incident, and some sensitive breaches are not public. It monitors important accounts, installs updates and reacts to real unauthorized activity. Don't pay for promises to delete all children from the Internet; once copied, the data can circulate in several places.

furt-de-identitate-protectie-pasi.excerpt: Identity theft is using your data to pretend to be you. Learn what information is being targeted, how to reduce exposure, and how to react when accounts, requests, or transactions appear that you don't recognize.
furt-de-identitate-protectie-pasi.seo_title: Identity theft: prevention and steps after the incident
furt-de-identitate-protectie-pasi.title: What is identity theft and how to protect yourself
furt-de-identitate-protectie-pasi.meta_description: Find out how stolen data is used, what preventive measures you can take and who to contact if you notice an impersonation.
furt-de-identitate-protectie-pasi.content:
Identity theft occurs when someone uses a person's data to impersonate themselves: they can try to take over an account, open a service, ask for money from acquaintances, or make transactions. Not every suspicious message or single unrecognized login confirms identity theft, but any specific activity you don't recognize is worth checking.

What data is used

Attackers can combine name, address, phone, date of birth, copies of documents, email address and passwords obtained from different services. A single detail may seem trivial; together, the data can help impersonate or guess recovery responses. Documents and selfies with documents are particularly sensitive. Send them only when there is a legitimate reason, to a verified recipient and through an appropriate channel.

Realistic prevention

  • Publish as little contact data, documents and information about your daily routine as possible.
  • Use unique passwords, MFA and a recovery address you control.
  • Regularly check your sessions, connected apps and alerts from your bank and service providers.
  • Securely destroy paper documents containing identifiers and do not keep copies of documents in sync galleries without adequate protection.
  • No send authentication codes to a person who calls you, even if they know some personal data.

What to do when you notice unauthorized use

Start with the affected account or transaction. Call the bank if payments or financial requests arise; ask for instructions on blocking the card, securing access and contesting operations. Change the compromised service password on a secure device and revoke unknown sessions. Check if your recovery data has been changed and secure your primary email before other accounts.

Contact the company where the fake account or claim originated using the contact details you found independently. Request blocking of unauthorized activity and retain the referral number. If there are indications of a crime, keep copies of messages, extracts and replies and contact the Police. If the incident involves computer access, reporting to DNSC can provide technical guidance. Procedures and remedies depend on the affected organization and the facts.

Beware of the second fraud

After an incident, some people may pretend to be investigators, bankers or money recovery firms and ask for upfront fees, codes or remote access. Confirm each request by calling the organization on an official number. There is no surefire way to guarantee a refund, and no one needs your password to file a complaint.

Keep a log of dates, accounts affected, people contacted and actions taken. It helps you not miss a recovery account and gives institutions a clear timeline. For complex legal or financial situations, ask for the advice of the competent institution or a specialist.

cum-verifici-telefon-compromis.excerpt: A dead battery or a slow phone has many causes and does not prove a compromise by itself. It checks apps, permissions, sessions, and alerts, and takes steps proportional to the clues it finds after a possible compromise.
cum-verifici-telefon-compromis.seo_title: How to check if your phone has been compromised
cum-verifici-telefon-compromis.title: How to check if your phone has been compromised
cum-verifici-telefon-compromis.meta_description: Check your phone's apps, permissions and accounts without jumping to conclusions from a symptom non-specific.
cum-verifici-telefon-compromis.content:
A phone that heats up, discharges quickly, or runs slowly isn't necessarily compromised. Updates, weak signal, a dead battery, and demanding apps can produce the same symptoms. Look for verifiable clues: an app you haven't installed, an unknown admin profile, unusual permissions, messages sent without you, or login alerts you don't recognize. A clue is worth checking, but it does not establish the cause by itself.

Basic checks

  1. Open the app list and remove apps you don't recognize or no longer use. Before removing, check that it is not a system or carrier component.
  2. Review permissions for location, camera, microphone, contacts, SMS and accessibility. An app should only have the access necessary for its function.
  3. Install available updates for the system and apps from the official store.
  4. Check sessions and devices connected to email, Apple Account, Google Account and messaging apps.
  5. Look at operator alerts about SIM, call forwarding or card change if you suddenly lose service.

Android and iPhone

On Android, the exact settings differ between manufacturers: look for "Privacy" or "Permission Manager" in Settings, check the privacy dashboard and Play Protect, and look at apps installed from external sources. Access to Accessibility, device management, or installation of unknown apps may be legitimate for some utilities, but it's worth reviewing if you don't remember granting it.

On iPhone, check Settings > Privacy & Security for app access and Settings > General > VPN & Device Management for profiles you don't recognize. Phones managed by work or school may have legitimate profiles; ask the administrator before deleting them. Check the list of devices associated with your Apple account and enable available lost device protections.

If suspicion remains

Updates the system, uninstalls clearly unknown apps and runs built-in security tools. If an account sends messages or transactions without your consent, secure it from another device and revoke sessions. If someone has installed remote control software, do not access the phone bank until you have reliable technical guidance.

Factory reset can fix some software issues, but it clears local data and doesn't necessarily fix the attacker's access to the accounts. Selectively back up important photos and documents, avoiding automatic restoration of apps you haven't checked. In cases of financial risk, threats or persistent access, contact the carrier, manufacturer or a specialist before resetting the device.

ai-nevoie-antivirus-windows-11.excerpt: Windows 11 includes Windows Security and Microsoft Defender Antivirus, but protection also depends on updates, settings, and habits. Learn what the built-in tools cover and when an add-on product might be useful.
ai-nevoie-antivirus-windows-11.seo_title: Do you need antivirus on Windows 11? Practical guide
ai-nevoie-antivirus-windows-11.title: Do you need antivirus on Windows 11?
ai-nevoie-antivirus-windows-11.meta_description: Find out what protection Microsoft Defender offers in Windows 11, what are the limits and when it makes sense to choose an additional antivirus.
ai-nevoie-antivirus-windows-11.content:
For many users, the built-in protection in Windows 11 is a reasonable starting point: the Windows Security app includes Microsoft Defender Antivirus, firewall, and other controls. However, there is no product that eliminates all risks. Protection depends on updates, active settings, app source, and how you react to suspicious login messages and windows.

What Microsoft Defender does

Defender can scan files and applications, detect known malicious behavior, and provide real-time protection when settings are active. Windows Update delivers system fixes; the Windows Security application shows the status for available viruses, firewalls, and controls. You can start a manual scan from Virus & threat protection when you have a specific reason, such as a suspicious file.

Check in Windows Security if real-time protection and security updates are active. If you install a third-party antivirus, Windows may change the product that manages real-time protection; avoid disabling a control without knowing what it replaces. Two overlapping solutions can create notifications and poor performance without automatically doubling the benefits.

When an additional solution may make sense

An additional product may be suitable if you have management requirements for work, use extra features that you understand, or need protection on multiple devices included in one subscription. Compare privacy policy, license term, performance and support procedure. Avoid windows that claim to have found dozens of problems before running a real scan and offers that pressure you to pay immediately.

An antivirus can't guarantee that a site is legitimate, it doesn't always stop you from entering your password on a fake page, and it doesn't cancel a payment you've authorized. An isolated alert is not proof that a file has been infected; verify the alert name through the product console and follow the vendor's documentation.

Habits that matter regardless of the product

  • Install Windows, browser and application updates without long delays.
  • Download programs from the manufacturer's website or official store and decline installers offered in unexpected advertisements.
  • Use standard user account for common activities when practical.
  • Back up regularly to a separate medium or a trusted service and periodically verify that you can restore files.
  • Use passwords unique and MFA for email and important accounts.

If you suspect a file, stop opening it and scan it with Windows Security. If the device shows persistent behaviors or you installed software at the request of an unknown person, disconnect it from your financial accounts and ask for reliable technical help. Choosing an antivirus is only part of a plan that includes updates, backups and careful verification of requests.

securizare-telefon-android-iphone.excerpt: A well-secured phone uses a lock screen, updates, limited permissions, backup, and methods prepared for loss or theft. The steps differ between Android and iPhone, but the principles are the same at home.
securizare-telefon-android-iphone.seo_title: How to secure your Android phone or iPhone
securizare-telefon-android-iphone.title: How to secure your Android phone or iPhone
securizare-telefon-android-iphone.meta_description: Set up screen lock, updates, permissions and backup to reduce the risks of theft and access unauthorized.
securizare-telefon-android-iphone.content:
The phone contains email, photos, conversations, and often access to financial accounts. You can protect it with a few simple settings, but there is no configuration that will prevent any theft or fraud. Start with screen lock and updates; then limit app access and prepare steps for loss or theft.

Lock the screen and protect the main account

Choose a PIN or password that other people can't guess from public information. Biometrics can be convenient, but keep a strong code as a backup method. Set automatic lock after a short period and hide the content of sensitive notifications on the lock screen. Avoid codes like 0000, year of birth or a visible pattern.

Your Google or Apple account controls your phone's sync, location, and recovery. Enable MFA, keep your recovery email and number current, and save your recovery codes in a separate, safe place. Periodically check the list of associated devices; only remove devices you can identify as unknown.

Updates and Apps

Enable automatic system updates and install apps from official stores. Check developer name, relevant reviews and permissions before installing. A flashlight app usually doesn't need contacts or a microphone for its function. Review access to location, camera, microphone, photos, and notifications; provide "only when using the app" permission when it meets the need.

On Android, look for Permissions Manager, Play Protect, and settings for installing from unknown sources; names vary by manufacturer. On iPhone, use Privacy & Security and check apps connected to your Apple Account. An admin profile on a work phone may be legitimate, so check with your admin before removing it.

Backup and anti-theft protection

Enable backup for the photos, contacts and documents you need, then check if you can restore the data to a new device. The synchronized backup is not the only copy; for important documents also keep a separate copy. Activate the official device location service and familiarize yourself with the lock, lost mode and remote wipe options. These features usually require setup before you lose your phone.

Apple offers additional protections in case your iPhone is stolen, and Android provides privacy and location controls that depend on version and manufacturer. Check your device's documentation; don't rely on a single menu name as the interface may change.

In case of loss or theft

Use the official tracking service from another device and mark the phone as lost if the option exists. Contact your carrier to lock your SIM and change passwords for important accounts on a secure device. Notifies the bank if the unlocked phone or banking app may be accessible. Do not go alone to a location indicated on the map and do not remove the device from the account if the official instructions say that you would disable anti-theft protection.

cum-creezi-parole-sigure-manager.excerpt: Long, unique passwords reduce the impact of a breach, and a manager can create and keep them secure. Learn to use passphrases without reusing predictable patterns for important accounts.
cum-creezi-parole-sigure-manager.seo_title: How to create strong and unique passwords
cum-creezi-parole-sigure-manager.title: How to create secure and manageable passwords
cum-creezi-parole-sigure-manager.meta_description: Create long and unique passwords, use a password manager and avoid reuse and composition rules predictable.
cum-creezi-parole-sigure-manager.content:
A good password is long, unique to that account, and hard to guess. Length and uniqueness matter more than the predictable replacement of letters with numbers. If the same password is used on multiple services, a breach in one of them can allow automated attempts on the others. A password manager solves the problem of memorization and can generate random passwords for each account.

Generate unique passwords

Use a reputable manager, protect it with a strong master password, and enable MFA if the service offers this option. Choose a master password that you don't use anywhere else; a long phrase made up of randomly chosen words may be easier to remember than a short string of symbols. Don't use a famous quote, family name, date of birth, or a sentence you've published.

Let the manager generator create different passwords for sites and apps. The supported length differs between services, so the generator may also provide a compatible variant. If a site asks you to periodically change your password without any hint of compromise, don't make up minor spins; change your password when it is exposed, reused, sent to someone, or when the service notifies you of a relevant incident.

Passphrases and examples

A passphrase is a longer combination of words. For an important account, select words randomly with the manager tool, not from a phrase that is easily associated with you. Examples like cat2026! or Password123 are just weak type warnings and should not be used. Attackers test dictionaries, common substitutions, and leaked passwords before trying completely random combinations.

Use the safe manager

  • Only install the app and extension from the official source and carefully check the domain before autofilling a password.
  • Enable MFA and keep the recovery code offline in a safe place.
  • Do not export passwords to an unprotected file and delete temporary copies after import.
  • Check for reused or compromised passwords in manager functions without sending passwords to sites unknown.
  • Plan recovery access if you lose your phone or encryption key.

A manager does not protect against a phishing page if you manually enter data there; autocomplete refusing a different domain is a practical signal though. For compatible services, consider a passkey, which does not require memorizing a password and is linked to the service domain. Do not share your master password via email or chat.

autentificare-doi-pasi-cum-activezi.excerpt: Two-step authentication adds a check on top of your password, but the methods offer different levels of protection. Learn how to choose between apps, security keys, passkeys, and SMS and how to prepare for recovery.
autentificare-doi-pasi-cum-activezi.title: What is two-step authentication and how do you enable it
autentificare-doi-pasi-cum-activezi.meta_description: Learn what 2FA means and MFA, how to compare apps, SMS and security keys, and how to keep recovery codes.
autentificare-doi-pasi-cum-activezi.content:
Two-step authentication (2FA) requires two verifications, and multifactor authentication (MFA) is the broader term for using at least two different categories of factors: something you know, something you have, or something you are. If someone gets the password, the second check can prevent access. However, protection depends on the method and how you react to unwanted requests.

Compare methods

Passkeys and security keys use cryptographic authentication linked to the service and are among the most resistant methods to fake pages. The passkey can be stored on the phone, computer or in a compatible manager; the physical key must be protected as an important object. Set up a recovery method before you lose your device.

Authenticator apps generate codes on the device and do not depend on the delivery of an SMS. Codes are sensitive though: a phishing page can ask for the code immediately and use it before it expires. Enter the code only on the site accessed independently and do not dictate it to a person who calls you.

SMS is better than password alone in many situations, but can be exposed through message forwarding, SIM switching, or operator tampering. If the service offers a more robust method, I prefer it for email, account management, and money. The appropriate method depends on what the account supports and your risk; enable any MFA provided instead of just being stuck with a reused password.

How to activate it without getting stuck

  1. Open the official application or website by typing the address yourself and enter Security.
  2. Choose your preferred method and follow the steps in the service; menu names may change.
  3. Add a second backup method if the service allows it, such as an additional key or an app on another device.
  4. Save recovery codes in a manager or offline location separate from the phone.
  5. Test the method on a trusted device before closing all sessions.

Unexpected requests and recovery

Don't approve a login notification you haven't started. Repeating requests can be an attempt to exhaust yourself until you hit "Approve". Reject the request, change your password if you have reason to believe it has been exposed, and check your recent activity. Keep your backup codes private: anyone who sees them can try to recover your account.

MFA does not stop all attacks. You can be tricked into approving a session or installing malware; combine it with unique passwords, updates and accessing services through the official app. Before you change your phone, transfer your authentication methods and verify the recovery of essential accounts.

ce-sunt-passkeys-parole.excerpt: Passkeys are cryptographic credentials stored on the device or synchronized through a compatible manager. They can simplify authentication and reduce the risk of a password being entered on a phishing site.
ce-sunt-passkeys-parole.seo_title: What are passkeys and how do they replace passwords
ce-sunt-passkeys-parole.title: What are passkeys and why are they more secure than passwords
ce-sunt-passkeys-parole.meta_description: Learn how passkeys work, why they are phishing-proof, and what to check for recovery and compatibility.
ce-sunt-passkeys-parole.content:
A passkey is a digital credential based on a pair of cryptographic keys. The service keeps a public key and the private key stays on your device or in a passkey manager. Upon authentication, you unlock the device with PIN, fingerprint or facial recognition; the key signs a challenge without sending a reusable password to the site.

Why it helps against phishing

The passkey is associated with the service domain. If you land on a domain that only looks like the real one, the browser shouldn't provide the same credential for the legitimate site. That reduces dependence on user attention and memorizing domains. Biometrics are used locally for unlocking; according to Google's documentation, biometric data remains on the device and is not sent to the company.

"Safer" does not mean invulnerable. If someone can unlock your device or get into the sync account that holds the passkeys, the risk changes. Protect your primary account with MFA, use strong locking, and don't create passkeys on a shared computer. For critical accounts, keep an additional recovery method that you can access.

Compatibility and synchronization

Support depends on operating system, browser, service and manager. Some passkeys can be synchronized between devices through the Apple ecosystem, Google or a compatible manager; others are tied to a hardware key or a single device. It does not assume that all services allow the same flow. See your account documentation and check what options are available before you remove your password or other factor.

How do you start

  1. Update your phone, computer and browser and enable screen lock.
  2. Access the official service manually and look in the security settings for "Passkeys" or "Access keys".
  3. Follow the creation instructions and confirm that the selected device or manager is yours.
  4. Add a recovery method and test authentication on another device if possible.
  5. Review the passkeys list periodically and remove credentials for devices you no longer own.

Passkeys are not the same as a code received via SMS or the manager's password. Learn how to regain access if your phone is lost. A passkey can be a very good choice for compatible accounts, and the password manager remains useful for services that have not yet implemented this method.

ce-stie-google-despre-tine-control-date.excerpt: The data associated with the Google account depends on the products used and the active settings. Review your history, location, personalization, and connected apps and download the information before you delete anything from your personal account.
ce-stie-google-despre-tine-control-date.seo_title: What data Google saves and how you control it
ce-stie-google-despre-tine-control-date.title: What Google knows about you and how you control the data collected
ce-stie-google-despre-tine-control-date.meta_description: Review your activity, location history, ad personalization and account data Google from Privacy Checkup and My Activity.
ce-stie-google-despre-tine-control-date.content:
What information is saved in your Google account depends on the services you use and your active settings. Search history, app activity, watched videos, location and profile data can appear in different controls. There is no single page that represents all copies of the data; also check each product's browser, device and settings.

Start with Privacy Checkup and My Activity

Sign in to your Google account by manually typing myaccount.google.com and open Privacy Checkup and My Activity. Review Web & App Activity, YouTube History, and Timeline where available. You can stop saving certain types of activity, set automatic deletion or delete a range. Settings may have new names or behaviors as Google updates them; read the explanation displayed for your account before changing your options.

Location history is not the only possible source of position approximation. Apps can use device permission and web services can infer an approximate zone from the IP address. Turning off a single setting does not automatically delete any data associated with all products.

Personalization and Ads

In your personalization settings you can control certain information used for personalized recommendations or ads. Opting out of personalization does not necessarily mean you will no longer see ads, nor does it remove data already saved. The settings are separate from the history you manage in My Activity and the data you keep in Gmail, Drive or Photos.

Download before deleting

If you want a copy, use Google Takeout to select the products and archive you want to download. Check where you save the archive: it may contain sensitive documents, photos and conversations. Keep it encrypted and delete the copy when you no longer need it. Before deleting a service or account, read what is lost and whether there is a recovery period.

Useful phone controls

Review the apps connected to your account and remove access to those you no longer use. Check location permission directly in operating system; a site can receive approximate location from IP even if it does not receive GPS coordinates. For shared devices, use separate profiles and log out when done.

Privacy review is a process, not proof that all data is gone. The Services need some information for operation, security or applicable obligations. Choose settings based on which features you use, export important data and check controls annually, especially after interface updates.

cum-reduci-urmarirea-pe-internet.excerpt: Sites can recognize visits through cookies, trackers and other techniques, depending on the browser and settings. Limit tracking through privacy controls, but don't confuse private mode with anonymity.
cum-reduci-urmarirea-pe-internet.seo_title: How to reduce tracking and online tracking
cum-reduci-urmarirea-pe-internet.title: How to reduce the tracking of your activity on the Internet
cum-reduci-urmarirea-pe-internet.meta_description: Limit cookies and trackers through browser settings and reputable extensions and find out what private browsing mode does not hide.
cum-reduci-urmarirea-pe-internet.content:
Online tracking can use cookies, browser identifiers, invisible pixels, connected accounts, and information you enter in forms. Some technologies retain your login or shopping cart; others help businesses measure visits across multiple sites. There is no button to stop all forms of collection without affecting some functions.

Control cookies and browser settings

In the browser settings you can block or limit cookies from third parties, delete site data and use the integrated protection against trackers. If an important site is down, grant an exception to just that domain and review it later. Deleting cookies may log you out and does not remove the records kept by sites on their servers.

Firefox, Chrome, Edge and Safari offer different controls; update your browser and consult the manufacturer's documentation for the installed version. Privacy extensions can block content, but can read page data based on the permissions granted. Installs few, from the official store, checks the author, updates and requested access and removes unused extensions.

Private mode does not make you anonymous

The private window reduces what remains in the local history after you close it and can separate cookies from the normal session. It does not hide the activity from the website accessed, the employer who manages the network, the internet provider or the services you log into. Downloads and bookmarks may remain on the device; the site may use the account, IP or other signals to recognize the session.

A VPN changes who sees your network connection, but it doesn't delete cookies or make you invisible to the accounts you're logged into. Block trackers at the browser level and use separate accounts if you want to reduce the connection between personal and professional activities.

Simple steps, no absolute promises

  1. Review cookie and tracker settings once a quarter.
  2. Limit location, notification, and camera permissions for sites.
  3. Use a separate browser profile for different activities.
  4. Log out of accounts when you don't need continuous customization.
  5. Don't install extensions that promise total anonymity and demand access to all sites without explanation.

Tracking reduction is a trade-off between convenience and control. Choose the settings you can keep, read consent notices and look for the privacy policy for services that receive sensitive data.

vpn-sigur-avantaje-si-limite.excerpt: A VPN encrypts the tunnel between the device and the VPN provider and can limit what the local network sees. It doesn't hide your activity from the sites you log in to and shifts some of the trust to the VPN operator.
vpn-sigur-avantaje-si-limite.seo_title: VPN: advantages, risks and real limits
vpn-sigur-avantaje-si-limite.title: Is it safe to use a VPN? Advantages and limitations
vpn-sigur-avantaje-si-limite.meta_description: Find out what a VPN protects, what information the provider can see and how to choose the service without promises of total anonymity.
vpn-sigur-avantaje-si-limite.content:
A VPN (virtual private network) creates an encrypted tunnel between your device and the VPN provider's server. On a public Wi-Fi network, this can limit what the network administrator can read about your traffic. Sites usually see the IP address of the VPN server, not your connection, but the services you log into can still identify you by account.

What VPN doesn't do

The VPN does not protect you from a phishing site, a malicious file, a stolen password, or a payment authorized by you. It does not delete cookies and does not prevent identification by account, browser or information you publish. Private mode and VPN solve different problems: the former limits local traces under certain conditions, the latter changes the route of traffic and who can see it on that route.

Trust moves to the provider

Without a VPN, your ISP can see certain metadata about your connections. With VPN, the VPN operator becomes an intermediary that can see network metadata and must process the traffic. HTTPS continues to encrypt the content between the browser and the site; The VPN should not be described as being able to read all HTTPS passwords, but it also does not make the VPN provider unable to see anything. Logging practices, jurisdiction, auditing, and incident response vary between providers.

How to choose a supplier

  • Read the privacy policy and find out exactly what login and diagnostic data they keep.
  • Look for verifiable information about independent audits, ownership, and fixed vulnerabilities.
  • Verify apps, updates, support, and payment method, not just “no logs” promises.
  • Avoid free VPNs with unclear business models and excessive permissions.
  • Use MFA on your VPN account and download the app only from the official source.

When it's useful

Can be useful to reduce metadata exposure to a local network or to connect to an organization's resources. It is not a universal requirement for every site access and does not replace updates, HTTPS, one-time passwords or account protection. Before you activate it, define what problem you want to solve and check if the chosen provider is suitable for that problem.

If you use a service VPN, follow the organization's instructions and don't install a personal product that interferes with it. For online privacy, combine several measures and treat any promise of total anonymity with skepticism.

securizare-cont-facebook.excerpt: Protect your Facebook account with a unique password, two-step authentication, and regular session checks. Prepare recovery methods ahead of time and watch out for fake support messages.
securizare-cont-facebook.seo_title: How to secure your Facebook account
securizare-cont-facebook.title: How to secure your Facebook account
securizare-cont-facebook.meta_description: Enable 2FA, check Facebook sessions and alerts, and prepare official account recovery methods.
securizare-cont-facebook.content:
Facebook account may contain conversations, photos and access to associated pages or applications. A unique password and two-step authentication reduce the risk of hijacking, and session checking helps you spot access you don't recognize. Meta menus are still changing; use Accounts Center and the official documentation for the path available in your application.

Strengthen authentication

Use a different password than you use for email and other networks. Enable two-step authentication via a security key, authentication app, or method available in your account. Keep your recovery codes in a safe place separate from your phone. Enable alerts for new logins and don't approve login requests you didn't initiate.

Check activity and recovery

In your security settings, check where you're logged in and disconnect sessions you don't recognize. Confirm your recovery email and phone number and remove old methods you no longer control. Review connected apps and sites; revoke access to those you don't use. Also check if contact addresses or page admins have been added without your consent.

Recognize fake support messages

A message may claim that the page will be closed if you do not immediately "verify" the account via a link. Do not enter the password in an open page in that message and do not send codes. Open the app directly and check the official notifications in your account. If you have a compromised account, use the official recovery flow from a previously used device, not an "agent" asking for money or remote access.

Reduce public information

Review your audience for posts, friend list, phone number and email address. Limit who can find or tag you and check posts where you're mentioned. Audience settings reduce visibility but do not prevent screenshots or redistribution by recipients.

If posts or messages appear that you didn't create, save the evidence, tell contacts to ignore requests for money, and secure the associated email address first. Changing your password may not close all sessions; manually check connected devices and apps. Check out the official help center if you can no longer log in.

protejeaza-cont-instagram-hackeri.excerpt: Secure your password, associated email and additional authentication, then check your activity and connected apps. Fake messages about copyright violations or support often try to steal account access. Prepare early recovery.
protejeaza-cont-instagram-hackeri.seo_title: How to protect hack Instagram account
protejeaza-cont-instagram-hackeri.title: How to protect your Instagram account from hackers
protejeaza-cont-instagram-hackeri.meta_description: Enable additional authentication on Instagram, protect email and recognize fake support and recovery messages.
protejeaza-cont-instagram-hackeri.content:
An Instagram account can be taken over by reusing a leaked password, a phishing message, or accessing the associated email address. Effective protection starts with securing your email, as it can receive reset links. Enable two-step authentication, check sessions, and only use the official recovery flow.

Protect your password and email

Use a unique password, stored in a manager, and change it if you entered it on a site other than Instagram. On the associated email enable MFA and check the recovery number, devices and forwarding rules. If someone controls your inbox, they can intercept reset requests even if Instagram has a new password.

In the Accounts Center, open the available security settings and enable additional authentication. Choose a method that you can recover and keep the codes offline. Review login sessions and disconnect devices you don't recognize; if you're not sure, change your password and then check again.

Beware of phishing messages

Scammers may send notices about copyright infringement, badge verification, sponsorships or account termination. They ask you to log in on an external form or send them a code. Do not reply via the link in the message. Open the app directly and check the notification section or account status. An urgent request does not become legitimate just because it uses the Instagram logo.

Review connected apps

Remove audience growth, scheduling, or analytics tools you no longer use and don't recognize. Some services require broad access for a limited feature. Check your granted permissions and change your password if you entered it directly in a third-party app instead of using official authorization.

If you lose access

Use the official in-app recovery page or Help Center and follow the available account checks. Operate from a previously used device and network if possible. Ask your friends to report the compromised profile and tell them through another channel not to send money or codes. After recovery, it removes unknown sessions and applications and checks if the email address and number have been changed.

Meta may change feature names and availability by region. If the menu has changed, look for "Security" or "Account Center" in the application settings and use the official help link, not the sponsored results that promise to recover the account.

recunoastere-frauda-whatsapp.excerpt: Scammers may ask for your registration code, money for an emergency or access via a link. Verify requests through another channel, enable two-step verification, and learn how to recover your compromised account.
recunoastere-frauda-whatsapp.seo_title: How to recognize fraud and fake messages on WhatsApp
recunoastere-frauda-whatsapp.title: How to spot fraud attempts on WhatsApp
recunoastere-frauda-whatsapp.meta_description: Don't share WhatsApp codes, check requests urgent through another channel and learn how to block and recover an account.
recunoastere-frauda-whatsapp.content:
WhatsApp fraud can come from a stranger or a friend whose account has been taken over. The messages often ask for urgent money, a verification code, vote for a contest or access a delivery link. Even if the name and photo are familiar, confirm unusual requests by calling the known number or in a separate conversation.

Never divulge your registration code

The code received via SMS allows the number to be registered on a device. WhatsApp explicitly says not to share it with anyone, not even friends or family. An attacker can claim to have sent the code by mistake or that they need it for a vote. If you receive it without asking for authentication, don't send it and enable two-step verification in your account settings.

A two-step verification PIN is different from a registration code. Don't send it to someone who says it's from support. Keep your current recovery email address if the feature provides it and use a unique password for the associated email.

Check messages from contacts

If a family member asks for money or data, call them using the saved number, not just a WhatsApp call from the same conversation. Scammers can take over real accounts and learn context from older conversations. Beware of offers that ask you to pay outside the platform, install a remote control app, or scan a QR received from a stranger.

Block and report

Don't reply to suspicious messages and use WhatsApp's report and block options. Periodically check connected devices and remove unrecognized web or desktop sessions. Photo, status and group privacy settings can limit spam, although they don't prevent all forms of fraud.

If your account has been taken over

Re-register the number in the official application with the six-digit code received by SMS or call; the WhatsApp documentation states that re-registration disconnects devices that were using the account. If you're asked for a PIN you don't know, follow the official process and waiting period indicated without paying a "retriever." Warn friends via another channel that someone may impersonate you, then check connected devices and enable available protections.

Do not delete the application before understanding the effect on the local backup. If someone requested money through your account, keep the captures and payment details; contact the bank quickly if you sent money.

primele-30-minute-cont-compromis.excerpt: Act in the order that limits the damage: secure your primary email, change credentials from a secure device, revoke sessions, and verify transactions and safely recover your compromised account, step by step.
primele-30-minute-cont-compromis.seo_title: Compromised account: action plan for the first 30 minutes
primele-30-minute-cont-compromis.title: What to do in the first 30 minutes after an account is compromised
primele-30-minute-cont-compromis.meta_description: Next steps clear after taking over an account: secure email, change passwords, revoke sessions and contact the bank.
primele-30-minute-cont-compromis.content:
The first few minutes after an account takeover matter, but rushing can lead to erasing evidence or changing the password on a still unsecured device. Write down what you notice and determine if email, a social account, a work service, or a financial account is affected. If there are transactions or access to money, call the bank immediately, even before going through all the checks.

Minutes 0–5: Limit access and preserve evidence

Stop chatting with the alleged attacker and don't send codes. Capture alerts, web addresses, and messages without redistributing links. If you have installed a remote control program or someone is controlling your screen, disconnect the device from the network and use another device known to change passwords. Do not reset your phone immediately if you need to keep evidence for your bank or employer.

Minutes 5–12: Secure your main email

Email is often the key to resetting other accounts. Access it by manually typing the official address, change the password to a unique one, and review the number, recovery address, sessions, devices, and connected apps. Check forwarding rules, filters, or delegations that you didn't create. Enable MFA and keep recovery codes separate from the phone.

Minutes 12–20: Secure Linked Accounts

Change reused passwords, starting with banking, social networks and work services. Use official recovery if you can no longer connect and report address or number changes you did not authorize. Revoke foreign sessions and access of unknown apps. Notifies the IT administrator if a work account has been affected; can block sessions and tokens that you cannot control yourself.

Minutes 20–30: check money and notify affected people

Look at recent transactions and call the bank if you've entered card details, approved a payment or noticed an unknown operation. Ask for blocking and appeal steps; the result depends on the method and time of payment. If a social account has sent money requests, alert contacts through another channel. Keeps referral numbers and history.

After this half hour, continue the recovery with the account provider and check the devices. If the incident involves a possible crime, report it to the Police; for cyber security incidents, use DNSC channels. Don't pay people who promise guaranteed recovery of your account or money and ask for an upfront fee.

cum-elimini-extensii-suspecte-browser.excerpt: Extensions can read or modify pages depending on the permissions granted. Check the author and requested access, first disable the suspicious extension and remove it from the web browser menu. It periodically reviews the list in all installed browsers.
cum-elimini-extensii-suspecte-browser.seo_title: How to find and remove suspicious extensions
cum-elimini-extensii-suspecte-browser.title: How to remove suspicious extensions from your browser
cum-elimini-extensii-suspecte-browser.meta_description: Check extension permissions and remove them in Chrome, Edge or Firefox; find out when it's worth resetting the browser.
cum-elimini-extensii-suspecte-browser.content:
An extension can add useful functions, but the permission to read or modify the data of visited sites can give it wide access. An unknown extension does not automatically prove an infection; check what you installed, who published it, and what permissions they have. If your browser started redirecting searches or showing unexpected windows, disable the extensions one by one and see if the problem goes away.

What you check before removal

Open the extensions page from the browser menu and note the name, developer, date of installation and permissions. Look for the exact name on the official store website and check if the extension is up to date and if the publisher is the expected one. Reviews can be manipulated and popular names can be imitated. Do not install a "scanner" from a window that appears on the suspicious site.

Chrome

Open the three-dot menu, choose Extensions > Manage Extensions, then disable the extension you want to check. If the symptoms disappear and you are not dependent on it, select Remove. In the Details page you can limit access to site data; grant access only when using the extension or only on required sites. Menu names may vary slightly by language and version.

Edge

From the Extensions menu, open Manage extensions. Turn off the switch to temporarily disable; for removal use Remove from the extension menu. Also check if an extension has been installed by an organization or device policy before you delete it from a service-managed computer.

Firefox

Open the menu, choose Add-ons and themes, then Extensions. You can disable the check switch or select the three-dot menu and Remove. If the remove button is missing, the extension may be managed by a device policy; ask the administrator for help instead of trying to circumvent the policy.

When you reset your settings

After removing the extension, check your search engine, homepage, site permissions and notifications. Resetting your browser can disable extensions and restore settings, but it can delete preferences or sessions. Back up your favorites and necessary passwords beforehand, and then reinstall only the extensions you need from the official store. If the extension reappears, scan your device with a trusted security tool and check for recently installed programs.
